ontology.title: One component concept, from architecture to behavior
ontology.summary: Components own child components, private data, functions and ports. Functions own calculations and flow or states. Solid arrows show ownership; dashed arrows show references. Requirements and cases describe intent; all views project the same model.
ontology.takeaway: Function means behavior with flow or states. Calculation means a pure expression. Component means one reusable software boundary with its own state.

nodes.title: Execution root
nodes.detail: A top-level component usage selects a concrete architecture. It can declare local behavior and child components inline, or instantiate a reusable definition with deployment bindings. Every instance, including the root, has its own store.

nodes.title: Component definition
nodes.detail: One software boundary owns private variables, functions, typed ports, child instances, connectors and delegations. The same rules apply to atomic and composite components.

nodes.title: Specialization
nodes.detail: A definition can specialize one base definition. It inherits effective members and may explicitly redefine compatible members. Child replacement must preserve its contract; cycles and silent overrides are rejected.

nodes.title: Child components
nodes.detail: A component owns zero or more component usages. Each usage instantiates a component definition, recursively. Reusing a definition never shares mutable state. Instances are created statically with the root.

nodes.title: Functions
nodes.detail: Functions own local calculations and flow or states. They may activate through a trigger or be called locally with call name(args), returning a copied value with as name. Inter-component calls use call port.member(args) with a timeout and failure path.

nodes.title: Calculations
nodes.detail: A calc belongs only to its enclosing function and is available in that function’s expressions, states and guards. It accepts explicit copied inputs and returns a pure expression value. It cannot capture mutable state or call executable functions.

nodes.title: Ports and routes
nodes.detail: Ports expose a versioned interface with a role. Connectors route between compatible ports, including an owned port and a child port. Delegation forwards a boundary to a child. Every exchange between distinct components follows an explicit route.

nodes.title: Deployment
nodes.detail: Deployment maps an instance path to an external target identity. A system URI or SysML part URI can be used without introducing a SWAML hardware classifier. Parent allocations apply to descendants unless overridden. No SysML import or conformance is implied.

nodes.title: Flow or states
nodes.detail: After optional calculation declarations, a function owns flow or states. Flow includes var declarations, bounded loops, decisions, assignments, calls, sends and returns. States own entry/exit actions, with guarded transitions and effects.

nodes.title: Value types
nodes.detail: Typed inputs, results, payloads and private data use bool, byte, uint, int, real and string, plus nominal records/enums and fixed-size arrays. void denotes no result. byte and uint have enforced numeric bounds; values are copied across boundaries.

nodes.title: Interfaces
nodes.detail: Interfaces describe data, events and callable function signatures. The four kinds are senderReceiver, clientServer, publishSubscribe and service. Component functions implement incoming behavior; an interface signature has no executable body.

nodes.title: Requirements
nodes.detail: Requirements express obligations with immutable typed attributes and one optional formal doc. Design elements claim satisfaction through satisfy.

nodes.title: Use cases
nodes.detail: useCase identifies intended use in a root context and may describe routed exchanges.

nodes.title: Verification cases
nodes.detail: verificationCase owns verify relations to requirements; docs describe the procedure. A relation is not a passed test.

nodes.title: Docs + comments
nodes.detail: A declaration can own one doc specification and many ordinary comments. Docs appear as compartments or table cells; comments are plain owned notes.

stages.title: 1 · Start with the user outcome
stages.summary: The use case describes the buyer’s intent. Production claims requirement satisfaction; a verification case identifies the procedure that must supply evidence.

nodes.title: Buyer: place an order
nodes.detail: Informative use case: a buyer submits an order and expects acceptance only after stock is reserved. The BrowserClient component models the communicating client; this story adds no actor or runtime element.

nodes.title: ReserveBeforeAccept
nodes.detail: The named requirement says: “An accepted order reserves stock before its confirmation and receipt are published.” It defines the intended outcome, not an executable function.
nodes.subject: WebShop::ReserveBeforeAccept
nodes.snippet: requirement ReserveBeforeAccept { doc /* An accepted order reserves stock before its confirmation and receipt are published. */ }

nodes.title: Purchase
nodes.detail: Purchase describes intended use through six routed exchanges and explicit dependencies. Design satisfaction belongs to Production.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Purchase

nodes.title: Production
nodes.detail: Production closes the topology of browser, application, inventory and mailer. Purchase references this root; the case does not create a parallel execution.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production

nodes.title: CheckPurchase
nodes.detail: The verification case specifies how to inspect the successful route and final stores. Its verify relation is intent; the linked simulator run is separate bounded evidence.
nodes.subject: WebShop::CheckPurchase

stages.takeaway: A user outcome becomes a named requirement and a route-valid scenario. Evidence remains a separate claim.

stages.title: 2 · Follow the routed message flow
stages.summary: Purchase describes the successful exchange order. Arrows below are case after dependencies, not additional software connectors or a measured execution trace.

nodes.title: 1 · Submit order
nodes.detail: The browser requests checkout. Actual endpoints are browser.checkout.submit → application.api.submit on checkoutLink. Delegation reaches application.checkout.api.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Purchase.checkout
nodes.snippet: call browser.checkout.submit -> application.api.submit via checkoutLink label checkout;

nodes.title: 2 · Reserve stock
nodes.detail: After checkout, application.inventory.reserve → inventory.api.reserve on inventoryLink. Delegation reaches inventory.stock.api; the request is handled by StockStore.reserve.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Purchase.reserve
nodes.snippet: call application.inventory.reserve -> inventory.api.reserve via inventoryLink after checkout label reserve;

nodes.title: 3 · Return reservation
nodes.detail: After reserve, the correlated Inventory.reserve result travels back through inventoryLink. The successful walkthrough uses quantity 2 against available stock 10.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Purchase.stock
nodes.snippet: reply inventory.api.reserve -> application.inventory.reserve via inventoryLink after reserve label stock;

nodes.title: 4 · Publish acceptance
nodes.detail: After stock, the case includes application.api.accepted → browser.checkout.accepted through checkoutLink. The event uses the service route in reverse; this row does not claim when the receiving handler completes.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Purchase.confirmation
nodes.snippet: publish application.api.accepted -> browser.checkout.accepted via checkoutLink after stock label confirmation;

nodes.title: 5 · Publish receipt
nodes.detail: After confirmation, application.receipts.created → mailer.input.created on receiptLink. ReceiptWorker.prepareReceipt owns the receiving handler.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Purchase.receipt
nodes.snippet: publish application.receipts.created -> mailer.input.created via receiptLink after confirmation label receipt;

nodes.title: 6 · Return acceptance
nodes.detail: After receipt, the correlated submit result returns through checkoutLink. BrowserClient.buy then records accepted. Its component lock can delay BrowserClient.confirmation until the request completes.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Purchase.result
nodes.snippet: reply application.api.submit -> browser.checkout.submit via checkoutLink after receipt label result;

stages.takeaway: Each exchange names an interface member, explicit connector and direction. Replies keep the request correlation; events have their own handlers.

stages.title: 3 · Open the checkout function
stages.summary: fv subject: Production.application.checkout.submit. Control flow stays inside CheckoutService; inventory.reserve uses its owned client port and explicit route.

nodes.title: Call inventory
nodes.detail: CheckoutService.submit sends a correlated request on its inventory port. Timeout, Unavailable, Rejected, Transport or RemoteFailure takes the terminating otherwise block.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.application.checkout.submit
nodes.snippet: call inventory.reserve(quantity) as reserved within 200 ms otherwise { return false; };

nodes.title: not reserved?
nodes.detail: A successful request can still return false. This guard separates refusal from acceptance without publishing a confirmation.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.application.checkout.submit

nodes.title: Return false
nodes.detail: The explicit otherwise and not-reserved branches return false. A timeout does not retract inventory-side effects that may already have happened.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.application.checkout.submit

nodes.title: Accept in statement order
nodes.detail: These four statements execute in this order inside the checkout component. Both publications are explicit publish statements on owned ports, with connector policy applied separately.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.application.checkout.submit
nodes.snippet: acceptedOrders = acceptedOrders + 1; publish api.accepted(orderId); publish receipts.created(orderId); return true;

nodes.title: Publication failure
nodes.detail: If either publish encounters rejecting admission, the activation fails without rollback. Stock, the acceptedOrders increment and any earlier admitted publication remain committed; this example has no distributed transaction.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.application.checkout.submit

stages.takeaway: Cases describe exchanges; functions implement decisions, private updates and explicit failure behavior. No automatic rollback is implied.

stages.title: 4 · Keep behavior with its owning component
stages.summary: Each card is a concrete component instance and lists its owned functions. A component can own private data and behavior together with child components; every function belongs to exactly one instance.

nodes.title: browser : BrowserClient
nodes.detail: Production.browser is a BrowserClient instance. buy requests two items, overOrder requests 99 and asserts rejection, and confirmation records the accepted event. Private data: lastOrder, accepted and rejectedOversize.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.browser

nodes.title: application.checkout
nodes.detail: Production.application is a WebApplication component instance. Its checkout child is a CheckoutService component. submit owns the flow shown in stage 3 and uses its owned api, inventory and receipts ports.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.application.checkout

nodes.title: inventory.stock
nodes.detail: Production.inventory is an InventoryService component instance. Its stock child rejects quantity <= 0 or quantity > available; otherwise it decrements its own available value and returns true.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.inventory.stock

nodes.title: mailer : ReceiptWorker
nodes.detail: ReceiptWorker.prepareReceipt receives the created event, records lastOrder and increments sent. It is a modeled receipt worker, with no undeclared external email transport.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.mailer

stages.takeaway: One reusable definition can appear at multiple paths; ownership and private data always belong to the selected instance.

stages.title: 5 · Read the resulting software structure
stages.summary: All four cards are immediate children of WebShop::Production. Named connectors join the shown owned ports; component cards expose their delegated component child.

nodes.title: browser : BrowserClient
nodes.detail: Component instance Production.browser, deployed on system:clientProcess. checkout is a requires port for Checkout 1.0.0. Requests flow outward; correlated replies and accepted events return over checkoutLink.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.browser

nodes.title: application : WebApplication
nodes.detail: Component instance Production.application, deployed on system:applicationContainer. Its api, inventory and receipts ports delegate respectively to checkout.api, checkout.inventory and checkout.receipts; delegation adds no queues.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.application

nodes.title: inventory : InventoryService
nodes.detail: Component instance Production.inventory, deployed on system:inventoryContainer. Its api delegates to stock.api. The stock instance owns available and reserve.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.inventory

nodes.title: mailer : ReceiptWorker
nodes.detail: Component instance Production.mailer is deployed on system:workerContainer. Its input port receives Receipts.created and activates prepareReceipt.
nodes.subject: WebShop::Production.mailer

edges.label: checkoutLink
edges.detail: browser.checkout → application.api; Checkout 1.0.0 requires → provides; qos RequestQueue: atMostOnce, fifo, capacity 16, overflow reject. Service events and correlated replies use the reverse direction.

edges.label: inventoryLink
edges.detail: application.inventory → inventory.api; Inventory 1.0.0 client → server; qos RequestQueue: atMostOnce, fifo, capacity 16, overflow reject. This connector has its own queues, independent of checkoutLink.

edges.label: receiptLink
edges.detail: application.receipts → mailer.input; Receipts 1.0.0 publisher → subscriber; qos ReceiptQueue: atMostOnce, fifo, capacity 32, overflow reject. Delegation reaches application.checkout.receipts.

stages.takeaway: Six descendant component instances, three explicit connectors and four external deployment targets form one closed root. Shared QoS values never merge queues.
